intro: This last unit brings the course together. First you will compare three very different societies, Germany, Japan and Mexico, on family, class, government, religion and what their own people say they value. You will see how each one faces shared challenges: paying for care through a welfare state, growing older as fewer children are born, and moving into giant cities.

Comparing whole societies is powerful and risky. Done well, it shows what is common to people everywhere and what is shaped by history and choice. Done badly, it turns real patterns into stereotypes. You will practice using evidence, words like many and on average, and the voices of people describing their own lives.

Then you will do the work historians and political scientists do. You will choose an open question, gather evidence from at least two regions, state the strongest case from both the left and the right, build a claim with evidence and reasoning, and answer the best objection. By the end you will be able to present an argument that is honest about the evidence and fair to people who disagree.
bigQuestion: What can careful comparison of societies teach us, and how do we turn that evidence into a fair, honest argument?

timeline.t: John Stuart Mill publishes On Liberty, defending free discussion and hearing both sides
Bismarck creates Germany's national health, accident and old-age insurance
Mexico adopts the constitution that still governs it, after the Mexican Revolution
Weimar Germany's democracy collapses as Hitler takes power
Mexico creates its social security institute, the IMSS
Japan's postwar constitution takes effect, making the emperor a symbol of the state
West Germany adopts the Basic Law, beginning with human dignity
A military coup ends democracy in Chile until 1990
Germany reunifies under the Basic Law
Mexico launches Progresa, a cash program tied to school attendance and health visits
A candidate from outside the PRI wins Mexico's presidency
Japan lowers its legal age of adulthood from twenty to eighteen

words.d: a government that uses taxes to protect people against risks such as illness, old age and job loss
the average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime
the growth in the share of a population that lives in cities
work not registered with the government, which pays no payroll taxes and gets no official benefits
a system with a monarch whose powers are limited or symbolic, while elected leaders govern
a fixed, oversimplified idea that all members of a group are the same
movement of people up or down between classes, during a life or across generations
a pattern in which two things rise or fall together, which does not by itself prove cause
unwritten habits and expectations that guide how people use power
stating the strongest, fairest version of an argument you disagree with
a reason or piece of evidence someone might use to reject your claim
a word such as often or probably that shows how strongly a claim is made

test.q: Which country's constitution keeps an emperor only as a symbol of the state?
test.why: Japan's 1947 constitution makes it a constitutional monarchy with a symbolic emperor.

test.q: Which statement about aging societies is supported by the unit?
choices: Fertility has risen across East Asia
About three in ten Japanese people are 65 or older
test.why: The unit cites World Bank data showing about 29 percent of Japan's people are 65 or older.

choices: A tax on all shops near churches
A fee for visiting a shrine
A tax paid only by Catholics in Mexico
A tax paid by members of registered churches, collected by the state
test.why: Members pay it, and leaving the church ends it.

test.q: In Esping-Andersen's typology, Germany is an example of which kind of welfare state?
test.why: Conservative welfare states, like Germany's, tie benefits to work and family.

test.q: What is the best evidence for what a society values?
choices: A popular movie from another country
How its own people describe their values, in surveys and in their own words
test.why: The unit stresses listening to people's self-descriptions and surveys like the World Values Survey.

test.q: Which sentence is a fair generalization rather than a stereotype?
choices: On average, households in Mexico are larger than in Germany
test.why: It names a measurable pattern and uses on average instead of all.

test.q: Why did Mexico limit presidents to one six-year term?
choices: Out of anger at long-ruling leaders before the Revolution
Because of a rule from the European Union
Because presidents are chosen by Congress
test.why: The single-term rule grew from resistance to leaders who held power for decades.

test.q: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source?
choices: Primary sources are always older than 100 years
A primary source comes from the time or people studied; a secondary source interprets it later
test.why: A census or law is primary; a history book about it is secondary.

test.q: Maya found that where American children grow up affects their chances of moving up. Whose research showed this?
test.why: Chetty's team found that upward mobility varies widely across American places.

test.q: Which is an example of confirmation bias?
choices: Checking a number against a second source
Searching only for studies that agree with you
Adding a qualifier to a claim
test.why: Confirmation bias means favoring evidence that fits what you already believe.

test.q: Which case shows that a modern, educated country can lose its democracy?
test.why: Weimar Germany's democracy collapsed in 1933 despite its education and industry.

test.q: What should a strong writer do with the best counterargument?
choices: Leave it out so readers do not see it
Mock the people who hold it
Replace it with a weaker version
State it fairly and answer it with evidence, a narrower claim or a concession
test.why: Answering the strongest objection honestly shows the claim has been tested.

test.q: The far left and far right both have extreme records. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Far left: the Gulag; far right: the Holocaust
Far left: the Holocaust; far right: the Gulag
Neither has any record of violence
test.why: The Gulag was Soviet Communist; the Holocaust was carried out by the Nazi regime.

test.q: Why is a claim with a qualifier like often usually stronger than one that says always?
choices: It matches what the evidence can support, so one exception does not break it
test.why: Qualifiers keep a claim honest about the limits of its evidence.

choices: Attacking a person instead of their idea
Honest disagreement while treating each other with respect
test.why: Civil discourse means disagreeing about ideas respectfully, listening and restating the other view.

write.prompt: Choose one capstone question: What best helps people move up? or Why do some democracies last? Take a position. Support it with at least two facts or sources from two different regions in this unit, state the strongest opposing view fairly, and explain why your claim still holds.
tips: Name every source: who made it, what it is and the year.
Give the strongest case from both the left and the right before you decide.
Use qualifiers such as often or on average, and avoid all and always.
Answer the best counterargument with evidence, a narrower claim or a concession.
Use the unit's terms, such as social mobility, norms and correlation.
